iterations.theme: Introduction, historical revisionism and the Second World War on Croatian soil (1939–1941)

sections.subtitle: A guest who speaks concisely: introduction to the discussion on historical revisionism
sections.screenshot_description: The host in the studio of the programme „Pogled s Markovog trga” greets guest Krešimir Rotim, who sits opposite him.
sections.content:
The programme **„Pogled s Markovog trga”** is broadcast from the Zagreb studio of TV Jadran. The host greets the viewers and introduces the guest, the young historian **Krešimir Rotim**, whom, as he points out, he often listens to because he „speaks briefly, but concisely”. The host remarks with humour that he himself usually talks at length with historians, and announces that this time he will try to have the guest speak more briefly about the topics before them.

In a short reply, Rotim thanks him for the invitation, after which the host comments that his name is recognised immediately in collegial and everyday circles, even by people who do not know him personally. The conversation thereby gains a frame: it concerns the public work of a historian whose views are spreading beyond traditional academic spaces.

sections.subtitle: From lecture halls into the spotlight: how history reached the wider public
sections.screenshot_description: Krešimir Rotim in conversation with the host; the programme title and the studio window are shown on screen while he speaks about writing and public appearances.
sections.content:
The host points out as the main merit of Rotim's work that history has, as he puts it, left the „closed spaces” of salons and lecture halls and reached **the mainstream and the spotlight**. He asks the guest whether this was a conscious intention or whether such a development happened spontaneously.

Rotim replies that he is himself part of the academic community: he studied history, published a number of scholarly articles and books, and took part in the centre of academic debates, although, as he says, he has not yet left a major mark. He stresses that he noticed arguments that do not get through and a narrative that does not pass, and that he followed the principle that the other side, which had not been heard until then, should also be heard. In his words, ideas today spread differently than before: once the struggle was waged with the pen, whereas today it takes place through video content and longer-format programmes, which allow for more argued and deeper presentation.

The guest claims that his views arise from in-depth analysis and many years of reflection, and from **archival material**, which he considers crucial for every historian. He criticises „mainstream” historians who, in his assessment, constantly keep Croatians in a tense atmosphere of guilt, and as an example he cites the debate with Goldstein, which, as he says, addressed geopolitical, security and historiographical questions. He believes that new media offer an opportunity for people to feel that „it was not as it had been written for decades”, that is, that there is also a Croatian side of history.

sections.subtitle: Revision as the foundation of science: from defending Stalin to the politicisation of history
sections.screenshot_description: The host asks a question about revisionism, while an illustration titled „Revizionizam u povijesti” (Revisionism in History) is shown on screen.
sections.content:
The host observes that the public believes all scholars may carry out revision except when it concerns Croatian history. When someone proposes that a topic should be investigated further, that person is, as he says, immediately labelled a „revisionist”, which in perception is equated with an enemy of the state. He asks whether this can really be so and how important revisionism in history actually is.

Rotim answers that **revision is the foundation of every science**, and especially of historical science, which, in his words, is burdened by politicisation. He points out that during the Second World War, the post-war period and the entire communist era, interpretations were deliberately shaped. As an example he cites the concept of antifascism which, according to him, Stalin introduced for the purpose of defending the Soviet regime, and which still contaminates the debate today. He adds that without revision there would be neither numerous scientific discoveries nor a general historical overview, and in his opinion this is a „method of disqualification” by which serious re-examination is meant to be prevented.

The guest also warns of the role of the media which, as he says, have the power of persuasion, and which some historians unsuccessfully try to use to shape public opinion. He concludes that it is important to address people with a creative approach, to present arguments concisely and thus to remove the stigma which, as he says, keeps Croatians in so-called silence.

sections.subtitle: „Croatian silence” and the price of open speech: reactions of the public
sections.screenshot_description: Krešimir Rotim sits at a table and answers a question about reactions, while the programme graphic is visible in the background.
sections.content:
The host comments that in Croatian public space people often speak of „Croatian silence” and that Rotim is one of the few who openly present their views, which, as he says, provokes a strong reaction from the other political pole. He asks whether it is difficult for him to cope with unpleasant and offensive comments on a personal level, and how he feels when he reads that people react to what, in his opinion, is factually based on documents.

Rotim admits that such reactions are sometimes laughable, especially when they come from neighbours to the east, but that it can also be unpleasant when someone tries to discredit him professionally while not being willing to engage in public debate. As an example he cites a situation in which, according to him, Hrvoje Klasić refused a face-to-face debate, and he assumes that after Goldstein's experience others will not dare to come to a public debate. He considers this bad, because public debate is the foundation of democratic life and, as he says, everything should proceed decently and without bitterness.

The guest stresses that he does not come into the public to scandalise or insult, but to revive historical moments and draw conclusions for the present. He regrets that, in his view, the left no longer has its former inclination to debate, and believes that today there is a lack of serious historians who would be ready for public debates and who, in the spirit of democracy, would seek a common denominator around national interests.

sections.subtitle: A continuity lasting a century: from Serbian policy before the First World War to the 1990s
sections.screenshot_description: The host speaks about the 20th century, while a map of the Kingdom of SHS with the period between the two wars marked is shown on screen.
sections.content:
The host points out that the 20th century is key to understanding Croatian history, and that the period of the Kingdom of SHS, followed by the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, clearly showed what later happened, but also **the continuity of a certain policy**. He states that he spoke with a colleague, Dr. Tihomir Rajčić, who deals with Serbian policy up to the First World War, and who, according to the host's words, repeatedly stressed that the ideas rooted in the Serbian political leadership before the First World War were in fact the same ideas that appeared in the 1990s.

The host concludes that the continuity is very clear and that history should be learned with understanding, not merely by heart. Rotim, in this part of the conversation, mostly builds on the need to view the wider context, stressing that events cannot be understood separately from what preceded them.

sections.subtitle: From the Cvetković–Maček Agreement to the Banovina of Croatia: the beginning of the unravelling
sections.screenshot_description: A document or photograph of the signing of the Cvetković–Maček agreement is shown on screen, with the name „Banovina Hrvatska” (Banovina of Croatia).
sections.content:
The host warns that the Second World War in the Independent State of Croatia is often discussed in fragments, so that from these fragments a story is created which is not complete. In his opinion, it is crucial to start from the events that precede the war. He names as the starting point **26 August 1939**, when the **Cvetković–Maček** agreement was signed and the **Banovina of Croatia** was created, which the host describes as a moment of political resolution and the breaking of state-legal ties. He adds that a special atmosphere arose in Croatia at that time.

Rotim adds that after the agreement and the creation of the Banovina, according to his interpretation, an attempt was made to partition Croatia. He claims that the role intended for Croats is clearly described in the documents of the **Chetnik movement of Draža Mihailović**. He stresses that the movement later split into several parts and did not have great strength, but that, in his opinion, it is dishonest to observe the Second World War only from 10 April 1941, without insight into the preceding events.

The guest adds that much has accumulated in the Western consciousness, including the fact that Stalin, according to him, was not in conflict with Hitler until 22 June 1941, and that both totalitarian regimes are responsible for the deaths of a large number of people, for which Rotim cites an estimate of millions. He stresses that all of this, together with the failure to confront the past, led to the legitimisation of the Stalinist order.

sections.subtitle: The „hunchbacked” coexistence of Croats and Serbs: the December Victims of 1918 as a symbol of resistance
sections.screenshot_description: The host speaks about the December Victims of 1918, while a photograph of Zagreb protesters from that period is shown on screen.
sections.content:
Rotim claims that after the creation of the Banovina an attempt was made to divide the area with the Croatian population, and that one can by no means speak of a common coexistence of Croats and Serbs as something to be cherished. As the reason he cites events in which, according to his words, Croatian politics and movements had to defend themselves against Greater Serbian pretensions, including the struggle against Italian encroachments in Dalmatia and Istria.

The host follows on that the common coexistence began „hunchbacked”, but that, in his opinion, it was not equally unfavourable for everyone. He recalls **5 December 1918** and the so-called **December Victims**, which, as he says, speak sufficiently for themselves. He describes how ordinary people in Zagreb rose to their feet against what they sensed was coming. He also mentions the enthusiast Trumbić who, according to his account, in 1920 in Italy and Japan banged his head against a wall when he realised that Pašić and Karađorđević were handing over Croatian territories to Italy, and that he came to his senses after that.

sections.subtitle: The assassination in the Belgrade assembly and the missing traces
sections.screenshot_description: The host speaks about research in Belgrade, while a photograph of the building of the Old Assembly is shown on screen.
sections.content:
The host describes the next impulse which, according to his words, shaped Croatian consciousness: the assassination in the Belgrade, that is, Yugoslav, assembly. He states that on the occasion of the ninetieth anniversary in 2018 he personally tried to investigate this event in Belgrade and that nowhere is there any trace of it. According to his claim, for Serbian, that is, Belgrade historiography, the event never happened. He describes that he visited both the Old and the New Assembly and made enquiries, but that there was no trace.

Rotim adds that one of the participants, according to his words, was released from prison after the outbreak of the war events. In the continuation the host refers to later assassinations, including the assassination of King Alexander I, and to the 6 January Dictatorship, stating that during the Yugoslav dictatorship thousands of Croats were killed by Serbian, that is, Serb gendarmes, from Lika to Herzegovina. In this context, in his opinion, the Independent State of Croatia emerges as an expression of the Croatian aspiration to its own statehood, which, as he says, Tuđman also stressed.

sections.subtitle: The proclamation of the NDH: advantages and disadvantages of the new state
sections.screenshot_description: Krešimir Rotim answers a question about the advantages and disadvantages of the NDH, while a map of the Independent State of Croatia is shown on screen.
sections.content:
The host asks a question about the advantages and disadvantages of the state established in 1941, after Croats, as he says, finally received their own state after centuries of wars and suffering. He asks in what this state was good and in what it went wrong.

Rotim replies that this is a complex question which would require a book, but that he will try to go layer by layer. He stresses that the state was an expression of the aspiration of the Croatian people, as Tuđman formulated it. He claims that the proclamation took place in several parts of the country, with examples such as the Bjelovar Uprising and the takeover of power in various places, including the Podravina region, Herzegovina, Dalmatia and Slunj. According to his words, the Yugoslav army was disarmed, there were no civilian casualties or revenge, and power was taken over before the arrival of the Germans.

As a positive element he cites the **spiritual and cultural awakening**: despite the state of war and the attempts of the Ustashas to ideologically take over almost all the threads of power, cultural life, as he says, came alive. Books were printed, writing about Croatian history was produced, and Croatianness was lived in everyday life. The Catholic faith was professed, while Orthodoxy, according to his interpretation, remained tied to the political projects of the Serbian royal authority, so that Orthodox inhabitants at one point, as he says, were not under the protection of the state. The guest thereby stresses that the negatives cannot be bypassed.
keywords: positive and negative sides of the state

sections.subtitle: The Holocaust, antisemitism and racial laws: what must be clearly separated
sections.screenshot_description: Krešimir Rotim speaks about the suffering of the Jews, and the host interrupts him with a question about racial laws.
sections.content:
Rotim warns that the question of the suffering of Jews must be separated from the question of the suffering of Serbs in Croatia, because, in his assessment, these are two different questions. He claims that the Serbian side cunningly mixes them, blaming Croats for everything and trying to link them with the Holocaust. He states that throughout Europe there was an anti-Jewish spirit which must be distinguished from the racial-biological teaching about Jews as an inferior race, because it has its own different laws. The suffering of the Jews, according to his words, is not disputed, but it was connected with pressures and legislation adopted by the state.

The host stresses that it must be clearly said that the Holocaust cannot in any way be justified. Rotim adds that nationalist thought at one point showed a certain tolerance towards Jews, with the note that there were also Jews in the Ustasha movement, and that the main journal of the Jewish community in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, according to his interpretation, wrote in a two-faced manner about Croats and King Alexander.

To the host's question whether adopting the racial laws was a mistake, Rotim replies that the justification given is that they were adopted in order to create a replica of the Viennese laws and to draw closer to the Germans. He claims that at that moment Croats, in his assessment, tried to secure their living space, especially in Dalmatia. He recalls that Mussolini recognised the NDH with a reservation about negotiations on borders, and that Pavelić, in his opinion, promised Mussolini nothing concrete. He concludes that the legislation was primarily motivated by adaptation to German laws, but that there was also a strong anti-Jewish climate which Croats must go through with their national conscience. He adds that implementation was not complete across the whole territory, but that a large part of the Jewish community was deported to Auschwitz, which, as he says, remains on the collective conscience.

sections.subtitle: Before 10 April: from the ambassador in Berlin to the accession to the Tripartite Pact
sections.screenshot_description: The host speaks about events in Belgrade on the eve of 27 March 1941, while the date „27. 3. 1941.” is shown on screen.
sections.content:
The host returns several days earlier than 10 April 1941 and warns that history does not begin on that date. He names the events of **27 March 1941** in Belgrade, mentioning General Simović and the Nobel laureate **Ivo Andrić**, who, according to the host's words, as ambassador of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in Berlin conveyed the news that Yugoslavia had acceded to the **Tripartite Pact**, that is, that Belgrade had taken the decision to stand alongside Germany.

The host also describes the demonstrations in Belgrade and other cities which, according to his claim, were instigated by British agents. He mentions that during his studies abroad he saw a photograph with the banner „better the pact than war”, but that in Yugoslav historiography, as he says, only a cropped frame was shown, whereas on the whole picture, according to his description, it was also visible that Chetniks with banners set off towards Croatia, with the intention of destroying and burning the Banovina of Croatia.

The host concludes that Belgrade's relationship with Croatia did not begin on 10 April, nor in April or May 1941, but much earlier, and that it culminated on 27 March. According to his claim, Belgrade would have been ready to destroy the Banovina of Croatia had the bombing of Belgrade and the break-up of Yugoslavia not occurred.

sections.subtitle: The demonstrations of 27 March and Serbian propaganda against Croatia
sections.screenshot_description: Krešimir Rotim speaks about diplomatic reports and Belgrade's attitude towards Croatia, while the host comments from the side.
sections.content:
Rotim and the host discuss archival sources. Rotim warns that many documents are located in Belgrade, while the Belgrade archives, according to his words, are still inaccessible, and that researchers therefore must turn to Western archives. The host mentions the Hoover Institution and the Smithsonian in Washington as places where, in his opinion, clearer sources can be found.

Rotim states that the Slovak ambassador in Belgrade said after 27 March that it seemed to him to be a restoration of Greater Serbia, and that this did not really look to him like some Yugoslav resistance. He also recalls the statements of the Croatian Club of Deputies after the assassination in the Belgrade assembly, which, according to his words, warned of the radicalisation of the political scene. He believes that such an atmosphere led to violence, including killings and beatings, and that no one answered for it, while Croats, in his claim, paid for their own bullets for their own killing.

The host adds that this situation is the product of a specific psychological climate in Europe which was more inclined towards undemocratic regimes. Rotim concludes that, unlike Austria-Hungary, in this area one does not deal with decent people with whom matters can be settled at the table, but with concealed motives and actions. He recalls that the Serbian Orthodox Church, in his assessment, actively helped unite Serbs in one state.

sections.subtitle: The revolt in Srb and ethnic cleansing: from Srb to Gospić
sections.screenshot_description: The host speaks about ethnic cleansing in the Krajina, while the parishes of Grahovo, Vrtoče and Krnjeuša are marked on the map.
sections.content:
The host describes a series of enclaves in which, according to his words, there was a revolt and a refusal to recognise the Ustasha authority, but also atrocities against the Croatian civilian population. He speaks of the „morbidly confused situation” from 27 July 1941 in Srb, which, as he says, continued until October 1941 in the wider area, including the entire Catholic parishes in Grahovo and further north-west. In his opinion, this is a classic **ethnic cleansing**, in which Belgrade, according to his words, does not want to recognise the Croatian state, regardless of what it was like.

Rotim adds that the revolt in Srb was prepared and planned, which can be concluded from the diaries, memoirs and collections of communist actors, for example in Drvar. He claims that Yugoslav soldiers did not want to hand over their weapons, but after the collapse returned home and did not hand them over for months, which, according to his interpretation, testifies to the planning of an armed uprising in line with the „Serbian mentality of armed solving of problems”. He also describes that the revolt caused a humanitarian catastrophe: children from Croatian areas, such as Boričevac and other places, moved towards Bihać and further, and columns of civilians, mostly women and children, were targets of shooting, due to which, according to his words, many people perished.

Rotim also states that the railway, as the main means of transporting food, was often occupied by insurgents or sabotaged, which further worsened living conditions. As one of the most difficult examples he cites the massacre of the Ivezić family, where the children, according to his words, were thrown into a pit. The host adds that the insurgents attacked civilians and not Ustasha garrisons, such as the one in Gospić, and that the parishes of Vrtoče and Krnjeuša completely disappeared. Rotim then refers to how the revolt is today celebrated in public, which he considers unacceptable.

sections.subtitle: Children from Kozara: shelters, documents and the dispute over „camps for children”
sections.screenshot_description: Rotim speaks about documents of shelters in Sisak, Zagreb and Jastrebarsko, while the host comments on the accusations of „camps for children”.
sections.content:
Rotim emphasises that the children who suffered in the revolt in Srb and its surroundings were placed in shelters in Sisak, Zagreb, Jastrebarsko, Gornja Rijeka and other places, and many families also in Požega and its surroundings. He states that the Croatian State Archives kept about 27,000 cards containing the child's name and surname, data on the parents, and whether the child ended up in a home or was fostered. According to his words, the procedure of care, which began on 27 July, was similar to that for the children from Bihać.

The host refers to the accusations coming from Belgrade about a „camp for children” and asks whether children were killed, whether there were gas chambers or similar crimes. Rotim answers that these were not camps for children but shelters, and cites as an example a document issued on the order of Maks Luburić, which, according to his interpretation, sends around eight hundred children and mothers to Požega, with the note that, because of the shortage of food, Orthodox families were feeding them. He considers this proof of a shortage, not of deliberate killing.

Rotim adds that the testimonies of nuns and state documents showed the catastrophic condition of the children on arrival. He mentions the testimony of Ante Dundović, who worked in the shelter in Sisak and testified before a communist court in 1945 or 1946, and who, according to Rotim's interpretation, described the starving children and the condition in which they were found, while the „politically correct” parts of that testimony, as he says, always had to be added. He also states that the child mortality was high, giving an estimate of around 20 to 30 per cent, with the note that one should not speak of figures concerning children. He rejects claims that nuns or workers of the Ministry of Health received instructions to kill or starve children, calling them exclusively a product of someone's imagination. The host comments that such morbidity is „from Serbia”, and Rotim adds that historians should write about this, including foreign authors such as Beader, with the note that memoirs are not the most reliable source.

sections.subtitle: Diane Budisavljević, Caritas and the myth of Stepinac: how a narrative is built
sections.screenshot_description: The host speaks about the role of the Caritas of the Zagreb Archdiocese and Stepinac, while the name „Caritas Zagrebačke nadbiskupije” is shown on screen.
sections.content:
The host refers to the film about Diana Budisavljević, which, in his assessment, minimised the role of the Caritas of the Zagreb Archdiocese and of Archbishop Stepinac. He states that it is said that she cared for about ten thousand children, and asks how it is possible that so many children could pass without anyone seeing or hearing about it, if the Ustashas were, as he says, „horrible”. He believes that such stories do not take logic into account and that irrational claims are put forward without verification.

The host claims that Caritas stood behind the entire operation and that Stepinac was involved and reacted. He stresses that the mythology about Stepinac often comes from Belgrade. According to his words, these stories claim that the NDH was the only state in the world that had a camp for children, which the host describes as „appalling” and as a policy built on the sacrifice of its own children so that others could be hated.

Rotim, in this part, agrees that the care of children was a complex process in which church and state institutions took part, and stresses that the documents showed a different picture from the one being put forward. He stresses that it is necessary to work systematically to have such claims verified and countered.

sections.subtitle: The Italian occupation of Dalmatia, Split and Istria: lost negotiations
sections.screenshot_description: The host speaks about Split and Istria, while Dalmatia and Istria are marked on the map as areas under Italian administration.
sections.content:
The host speaks of a part of the public in Dalmatia which, according to his words, is well acquainted with the story of the surrender of Dalmatia and Istria. He says that Split and Istria fared badly and that people were thrown into the hands of the Italians, which, in his opinion, explained the emergence of the resistance movement and the Split detachments that later called themselves partisan. He believes that living under the Italians was not possible and that in Split he felt „gigantic fascism”.

The host states that in the negotiations it had been agreed that Split would have dual government, Italian and Croatian, but that this was not implemented. Rotim adds that Mussolini did not keep the agreement. According to his claim, the fascist regime, after its defeat in the African colonies, sought an expansion through which it would achieve its planned „Roman Empire”. He claims that totalitarian regimes believe they are the bearers of historical progress, and that fascism, in his assessment, tried to take advantage of the opportunity, although militarily it was not particularly successful, but it caused enough confusion.

Rotim concludes that the NDH should be viewed through two layers: on the one hand, unnecessary reprisals and crimes committed by the authorities, and on the other, the Croatian state as a project. The host agrees that this should be clearly separated and warns that the Croatian people are not violent by nature, but that there were people of various political ideas in the army and administration.

sections.subtitle: The Rome Agreements and the military balance of power: agreements with the Chetniks as a strategic move
sections.screenshot_description: Krešimir Rotim speaks about the Rome Agreements, while a text or photograph of a document from 1941 is shown on screen.
sections.content:
Rotim claims that the Rome Agreements were the consequence of military pressure and the strength of the Italians, who had around 200,000 soldiers in this area. In his assessment, Croatia achieved as much as could be achieved, although the agreements were not largely respected. He states that the Italians immediately began to cooperate with the Chetniks, so that, according to his interpretation, a situation arose in which the Black Legion, the partisans and the Chetniks cooperated with the Italians, with everyone connecting with everyone, but no one was strong enough for the others to fear.

Rotim also states that Tihomir Dretzgu, a lawyer, wrote in the press of the time that the agreements were annulled because they were not respected. According to his words, the lawyer pointed out that something not drawn up in good will and under pressure can hardly be legally sustained. Rotim believes that Pavelić invited the Croatian national leaders to the negotiations, including Eduard Bulat, and that Croatia was too weak to achieve deeper political goals. The host adds that internal problems were eating away at the state and that politics was largely improvised under wartime conditions.

Rotim then explains that in 1942 agreements with the Chetniks began in north-western Bosnia, which, as he admits, seems astonishing to many, given that, according to his words, the same Chetniks tried to ethnically cleanse Croats. He believes that the strength of Croatian institutions south of the Sava was questionable, and that because of this things had to be improvised on the ground. He also states that the question of violence and reprisals in the NDH must be further investigated.

sections.subtitle: Revenge, reprisals and the question of the responsibility of the Croatian authorities
sections.screenshot_description: The host and Krešimir Rotim discuss revenge and reprisals, while a photograph from the period of the NDH is shown on screen.
sections.content:
Rotim stresses that the questions of violence, crimes and reprisals in the Independent State of Croatia are among the most controversial and that there is much myth and lies in them. He states his view that the Croatian authorities, especially in the summer of 1941, should and could have suppressed more the revenge and reprisals which, according to his words, were started by the Serbs. However, he adds that in such situations one must not play by the rules of the opponent, and that every person has the right to dignity.

The host recalls that Tuđman had already strongly insisted in 1990 and 1991 that there should be no revenge of any kind. The host concludes that history must be learned from, and announces a shorter break in the programme and a continuation of the conversation, with the announcement that the next part will deal with 1941 and 1942 and with Lordan, who, as he says, is mentioned in public.

iterations.theme: Children from Kozara, camps and shelters, Jasenovac, the film by Lordan Zafranović and a concluding reflection on the Homeland War

sections.subtitle: After the break: Kozara, children and the question of who is responsible for their fate
sections.screenshot_description: The host in the studio after a short break announces the continuation of the conversation with guest Krešimir Rotim, with a graphic bearing the title of the topic „Kozara i djeca”.
sections.content:
After a short break the programme continues in the Zagreb studio of TV Jadran. The **host** announces that the conversation will now focus on one of the hardest topics from the period of the Independent State of Croatia: the fate of the children from Kozara. He reminds that in this part of the story it concerns a confused situation on the ground, where several conflicts and interests intertwine in the period 1941 and 1942.

The host stresses that in this area, alongside the Ustasha authorities, partisan, Chetnik and Italian influences were active, so that events cannot be followed through a single narrative. According to his account, more than two thousand children from Kozara were received into Croatian families, while for a larger number of children it is stated that they reached Belgrade, where, according to the claims the host presents, they were rejected and returned, and then placed in Croatian families. The host stresses that these data, in his opinion, are contained in archival material.

**Krešimir Rotim** further clarifies the context and agrees that without understanding the military and political framework it is not possible to understand the fate of the children. The guest warns that stories about children are often used for political messages, so it is necessary to return to the documents.

sections.subtitle: Why did families with children go into the forest? The question of causes and the armed revolt
sections.screenshot_description: A close-up of the host asking a question, with a map of the Kozara area and Srb, marked with the revolt locations, shown in the frame.
sections.content:
The central question of this part of the programme was why parents, with their children, went into the forest and joined the armed resistance. The **host** asks what motivates families to lead such a life with children in the forest, in conflict with the country in which they live. He asks also whether these were Orthodox Serbs, where the weapons came from, and what led to such a situation.

**Krešimir Rotim** answers that the causes cannot be reduced to a family decision. In his opinion, he sees the main cause in „successful communist agitation” and in the general hostility towards the Croatian state. As an example the guest cites the Poglavnik's order on clearing the insurgent localities before the offensive on Kozara, which he describes as humanitarian in motivation, claiming that it aimed to protect women and children, while the struggle was waged only against persons carrying weapons.

Rotim further describes that the insurgents, according to his words, created strongholds and tried to establish a wider zone of control, and that such a situation, combined with the strategic importance of the area, inevitably led to a military reaction. In this context the host adds that the insurgents attacked civilians and not Ustasha garrisons, which Rotim confirms by claiming that the insurgents appeared when, in his opinion, they felt ready. The guest refers in doing so to the diaries of prominent communists who, according to his words, were preparing the revolt.

sections.subtitle: Humanitarian catastrophe and the path of the children: from Jasenovac to Zagreb
sections.screenshot_description: A display of an archival card index of the Croatian State Archives with cards of children, under the inscription „Hrvatski državni arhiv”.
sections.content:
Rotim describes that the first major humanitarian catastrophe, which struck children most, was a direct consequence of the revolt. According to his account, children from Croatian areas, including places such as Boričevac, set off towards Bihać and further, while a civilian column, mostly women and children, was exposed to gunfire. The guest claims that a large number of people perished in this.

According to his words, the children were initially placed in places in the vicinity of Jasenovac, and then news of their catastrophic condition reached Zagreb. From 27 July, Rotim continues, the care of children was started through homes and later families, according to a procedure which, in his account, was basically similar for all.

The guest stresses that anyone can check these data in the **Croatian State Archives**, where, according to his words, more than 27 thousand cards are located. Each child, he claims, has recorded name and surname, data on the parents, and whether the child ended up in a home or was fostered. The host confirms the importance of these sources, and Rotim stresses that the truth about the children must be based on documents and not on subsequent interpretations.

sections.subtitle: Fostered children and the Serbian interpretation: „criticisms” that do not fit the documents
sections.screenshot_description: A medium shot of the guest speaking in the studio, with a graphic reading „Srbijanska interpretacija” and a comparison of documents.
sections.content:
Rotim addresses the question of fostering children in Croatian families. According to his account, the eastern neighbours criticise this practice, claiming that the children were fostered in Catholic families and that the children themselves were not Catholics. The guest describes this as part of a wider „industry of historical memories” which, in his view, has been developing in Serbia for decades.

Rotim claims that such claims are not in line with the documents which, as he says, „every reasonable person” can check. However, he adds that, in his words, the documents in the Serbian discourse are interpreted selectively or even presented as falsified.

The host follows with the announcement that the conversation will then move on to more concrete examples, including the role of particular institutions and persons. In this part of the programme the guest especially emphasised that distinguishing between documented aid and political propaganda is crucial for understanding the whole story.

sections.subtitle: Caritas, Diana Budisavljević and Archbishop Stepinac: who really saved the children?
sections.screenshot_description: A photograph or archival display of Diana Budisavljević with the inscription „Caritas Zagrebačke nadbiskupije” and a portrait of Archbishop Stepinac.
sections.content:
The host opens the question of the role of the **Caritas of the Zagreb Archdiocese**, **Diana Budisavljević** and Archbishop **Alojzije Stepinac** in the care of children. He states that there was a film about Diana Budisavljević, but that in it, in his view, the role of Caritas and of Stepinac himself is marginalised. According to his words, it is stated that about ten thousand children were cared for, which the host considers almost incredible given the circumstances of the time.

The host asks a rhetorical question: how is it possible that such a number of children could be cared for and „walked out” without anyone seeing or hearing about it, and why is all credit attributed to a single person. He points out that people often speak of the „bloodthirsty” Ustashas and of Stepinac, so the question arises as to how in such an atmosphere it was possible to organise aid.

**Krešimir Rotim** confirms that Caritas, in his opinion, was behind the entire process, and that Stepinac was involved and reacted. The guest believes that the question of Stepinac and Caritas has often been reduced to a one-sided picture, so it is necessary to take into account the entire context and documentation.

sections.subtitle: The myth of the „camps for children”: shelters in Sisak, Zagreb and Jastrebarsko
sections.screenshot_description: A map of Croatia with Sisak, Zagreb, Jastrebarsko, Gornja Rijeka and Požega marked, and the inscription „Prihvatilišta, a ne logori” (Shelters, not camps).
sections.content:
One of the central parts of the conversation concerned claims about „camps for children”. The host states that it is often claimed from Belgrade that the Independent State of Croatia was the only state in the world that had a camp for children. He describes this as a policy which, in his words, is built on the sacrifice of its own children so that others could be hated.

**Krešimir Rotim** answers that in this case it is not a question of camps, but of **shelters**. He names Sisak, Zagreb and Jastrebarsko as places, and mentions Gornja Rijeka as well as many other places. He adds that many families were also placed in Požega and its surroundings.

Rotim refers to the claim that the children in the shelters had to be cared for in very difficult conditions, and that the question of alleged murders and poisonings, which is often mentioned, cannot be confirmed by documents. The host and the guest conclude that the presentation of these institutions as places of mass suffering is, in their opinion, unfounded.

sections.subtitle: The order on placing children, testimonies and the question of mortality
sections.screenshot_description: A copy of the order signed by Maks Luburić, titled „Smještaj djece” (Placement of Children), with an excerpt from a testimony.
sections.content:
Rotim refers to an order signed by **Maks Luburić**, which, according to his interpretation, concerns the sending of a large number of children and mothers to Požega. The guest stresses that the order states, because of the shortage of food, that the children could also be fed by Orthodox families. Rotim cites this detail as proof that it was an attempt at care and not planned destruction.

As testimony he cites **Ante Dundović**, who worked in the shelter in Sisak and testified before a communist court in the mid-1940s. Rotim claims that the children arrived in a starved and difficult condition, which, in his opinion, was the consequence of the revolt and forced removal into the forest. He adds that such verdicts must be viewed in the context of their time.

On the question of mortality the guest presents estimates which, according to his words, arose from his own analysis and sources. At different moments he cites different percentages of child mortality, with the note that one cannot be certain of the exact figure and that this was a wartime year. The host comments that speaking of figures for children is morbid, while Rotim claims that such a discussion is necessary in order to reject accusations of deliberate starvation and killing.

sections.subtitle: Croatian diplomacy without coordination: the lack of a plan and the role of memoirs
sections.screenshot_description: A close-up of the host commenting, with a graphic reading „Ministarstvo vanjskih poslova” (Ministry of Foreign Affairs).
sections.content:
Rotim criticises the fact that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in his view, has no clearly defined way of working when it comes to sensitive topics, especially when Croatia is accused of having had a concentration camp for children. The guest claims that such a situation requires serious coordination, but that, according to his words, this is not visible.

As an example of ignorance of sources he cites a case in which, according to him, one interlocutor used memoirs as the main source. Rotim claims that memoirs rank third in the hierarchy of historical sources and that the claims of prominent politicians must be interpreted with caution, since in their recollections they may distort or pass over facts.

The host agrees that Croatia must work on making its own institutions aware of the existence of policies with which normal communication is not possible, and that without a systematic approach Croatia remains on the defensive.

sections.subtitle: The Jasenovac exhibition at the UN: 700,000 victims and the need for Croatian personnel
sections.screenshot_description: A photograph of the United Nations building in New York, with the Jasenovac exhibition shown.
sections.content:
The host refers to the exhibition on Jasenovac which, according to his words, Serbia set up at the headquarters of the **United Nations** shortly before the General Assembly. He states that the exhibition, in which the figure of 700 thousand victims of Jasenovac is mentioned, had been up for about six months, while the Croatian delegation, according to his words, had no idea what was happening.

Rotim and the host conclude that Croatia must first clearly answer for itself the question of how to address international public opinion. The host concludes that Croatia needs **Croatian personnel** in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and in embassies, that is, people who, as he says, protect the interests of their own country and do not engage in conflicts without foundation.

The host assesses that this is a matter of basic institutional preparation and that a reaction cannot be based on improvisation but on systematic work from the foundations up.

sections.subtitle: The film by Lordan Zafranović: financing, political background and the „monstrous” work
sections.screenshot_description: A poster or frame from the film by director Lordan Zafranović, with the inscription „Financiranje i politička pozadina” (Financing and political background).
sections.content:
The host turns to the film by **Lordan Zafranović** and its financing. According to his words, the film was financed from Serbian sources and allegedly also with money from the **Serbian Orthodox Church**. The host states that the director, according to his own statements, dedicated his work to Patriarch **Porfirije**.

The host considers that Zafranović created a „monstrous” work, not a monumental one, and that it uses authentic names from history but attributes to them invented characteristics and actions. In his opinion, the film presents itself as a feature film, whereas in fact it is a construction that meets the criteria neither of a feature film nor of a documentary.

The host also states that the film, according to his words, is hard to place outside Serbia, that is, at international festivals. He adds that certain actors, according to his claims, joined the pre-election campaign, and comments that the rhetoric in Serbia has not essentially changed in recent years.

sections.subtitle: The director's statements and the public reaction: from the „Ustasha flat” to personal comments
sections.screenshot_description: A recording of the host in the studio commenting on the director's statements, with a sign reading „Ulica Brune Bušića” (Brune Bušić Street) shown.
sections.content:
The host comments on interviews the director gave in which, according to his words, he speaks not so much about the film as about his departure from Croatia in 1991. He states that the director claims he had to flee from the Ustashas, and that because of this he received a flat in Zagreb in a part of the city which the host ironically describes. The host assesses this claim as unserious and offensive, especially given the themes with which the film deals.

The host compares the director's statements with the work of other authors, and particularly emphasises that these are matters which, in his opinion, go beyond the framework of serious debate.

**Krešimir Rotim** states that the director's motives seem to him hard to understand, unless they are down-to-earth, that is, linked to money and power. The guest believes that with these moves the director, in his opinion, is harming his own reputation and that part of the Croatian acting scene which took part in it.

sections.subtitle: Croatia and Serbia: the missing, war reparations and accession negotiations with the EU
sections.screenshot_description: A graphic with the inscriptions „Nestali” (The Missing), „Ratna odšteta” (War Reparations) and „Pristupni pregovori s EU” (Accession Negotiations with the EU), with a brief display of the flags of Croatia and Serbia.
sections.content:
Rotim refers to the relations between Croatia and Serbia and stresses that the current talks concern the question of missing persons and war reparations. According to his words, Croatia, alongside archival material, should insist on the return of documents, but these obligations, in his view, already arise from the contractual frameworks.

The guest concludes that Croatia has the opportunity, within its membership of the European Union, to block certain steps which would be favourable to Serbia if the mentioned questions are not resolved. He believes that Serbia's attitude towards Croatia and its institutions remains burdened by political incitement, and that such rhetoric is reactivated each time internal problems appear in Serbia.

Rotim additionally claims that the Serbian political elites, in his opinion, are trapped in the concept of Greater Serbian politics, which makes normalisation of relations difficult. The host agrees with the assessment that Serbia, in this context, is a place where, in his view, wider geopolitical processes also unfold.

sections.subtitle: Announcement of a special programme on Jasenovac and the question of a monumental film about the Homeland War
sections.screenshot_description: The host in the studio with the inscription „Najava posebne emisije: Jasenovac” (Announcement of a special programme: Jasenovac) and a short introduction to the topic of the Homeland War.
sections.content:
The host announces a special thematic programme on **Jasenovac**, in which, as he says, the guest will have the opportunity to present his positions in more detail. He states that Rotim is very strong on this topic, and that the conversation about it will be held in a separate edition.

The host then asks why Croatia, in his view, has so far not made a truly **monumental film about the Homeland War**. He stresses that there are many heroic stories and dramatic events which, in his opinion, could serve for a powerful film presentation.

The host claims that this question should also be viewed from the perspective of the audience, since, according to his words, young people today read books less often and inform themselves more often through short video content. He concludes that a film could remain in memory much longer than a book.

sections.subtitle: Financing of cinematography and national historiography: what should be done
sections.screenshot_description: A guest in the studio speaks about legal regulation, with a graphic reading „Financiranje kinematografije” (Financing of Cinematography).
sections.content:
The host and the guest discuss the difference in the financing of cinematography. The host states that the Serbian film centre, according to his words, is financed from state funds and that money is given exclusively for national and historiographical subjects, while Croatia, in his opinion, finances a broad range of content, including Yugoslav cinematography.

**Krešimir Rotim** believes that in such a situation no change can be expected without legal regulation. He proposes that the law prescribe how much domestic music must be on public airwaves, and that the manner in which Croatian history of the Homeland War is presented also be regulated more clearly.

The guest stresses that this is a matter of political and cultural responsibility, and that such solutions should be realised when opportunities arise within the administrative structures of the Republic of Croatia.

sections.subtitle: Closing remarks: belonging to the generation that inherits freedom and a message about patriotism
sections.screenshot_description: A close-up of the guest in the studio as he concludes the conversation, with the inscription „Rodoljublje i domoljublje” (Patriotism and Love of Homeland).
sections.content:
In the closing part of the conversation **Krešimir Rotim** speaks as a member of a generation which, as he says, inherits the freedom won in the Homeland War. He stresses that he carries this in his heart and that, if an opportunity arises, questions of Croatian history and cinematography will be resolved in a manner which, according to his words, many in Croatia expect.

The guest concludes with an optimistic message that Croatia is heading in a good direction, that Serbian claims are increasingly less accepted, and that the public is no longer prepared to remain silent. The host joins him in the conclusion that Croats should speak openly about their history.

sections.subtitle: Domoljublje, rodoljublje and thanks to the guest: the end of the programme
sections.screenshot_description: The host in the studio with the inscription „Pogled s Markovog trga” as he announces the next edition and greets the viewers.
sections.content:
The host thanks the guest for taking part and wishes him much happiness and success. In his closing comment he emphasises the importance of **healthy patriotism** and **love of homeland**, with the claim that Croats should openly express love for their people, without fear of being labelled.

The host also presents the view that love of homeland and patriotism are fine categories which, in a negative context, are sometimes equated with nationalism, and recalls that the United States of America, according to his words, also rests on strong patriotism.

The programme ends with an announcement of the next edition, in which the topics only opened in this conversation should be continued, including Jasenovac.
